q.q: What is a flat file database?
o: Data held in several tables linked by keys
All the data held in one table, one row per record
A table that has been normalised to 3NF
A database with no primary key in any table
q.why: A flat file holds everything in one table, so details are typed again and again.

q.q: What is the main cause of data inconsistency in a flat file system?
o: Using a primary key that is too long to type correctly
The same data stored in several places and not all copies updated
Too few records in the file for the data to be useful
Fields given the wrong data type when the file was set up
q.why: Inconsistency arises when duplicated data is updated in some places but not others.

q.q: In a relational database, how are two tables linked?
o: Both tables are sorted on the same field
Both tables are stored in the same file on the server
A foreign key in one table matches the primary key of the other
Both tables are given the same primary key field name
q.why: A foreign key holds values of another table's primary key, creating the relationship.

q.q: For which situation is a flat file most appropriate?
o: A hospital's patient records used by many wards
A teacher's single list of names for a school trip
An online shop with orders, products and customers
A bank's account system used by hundreds of staff
q.why: A small single-user list with no related data gains little from a relational design.

q.q: Which of these is a main feature of a relational database?
o: All data is stored in one large table for fast searching
Each record is stored in its own separate file
Each fact is stored once, so an update is made only once
Every table must have the same fields as the others
q.why: Storing each fact once minimises redundancy and means updates are made in one place.

q.q: How does a DBMS stop two users overwriting each other's changes to the same record?
o: It deletes the record and asks both users to re-enter it
It only lets one user log on at any one time
It gives each user a separate copy of the database
It locks the record while one user updates it
q.why: Record locking lets many users share the database safely.

q.q: A DBMS gives users access rights by role. What do these rights control?
o: Which data types each field is allowed to hold
Which relationships may be drawn on the ER diagram
Which primary keys may be copied as foreign keys
Which operations, such as SELECT or DELETE, each user may perform
q.why: Access rights decide which of SELECT, INSERT, UPDATE, DELETE, ALTER and CREATE each user can do.

q.q: Which item belongs only in a physical data model?
o: The attributes of each entity
The relationships between entities
The entities to be stored
The data type and size of each column
q.why: Data types depend on the DBMS, so they belong in the physical model.

q.q: Which statement about a logical data model is correct?
o: It is independent of the database software
It is written for one specific DBMS
It lists the indexes for each table
It is produced after the database is built
q.why: The logical model is a design-stage model of the data requirements, the same whatever DBMS is used.

q.q: Why might two physical models built from the same logical model differ?
o: They are built for different DBMSs with different data types and features
One of them must contain an error in its relationships
They describe the data requirements of different organisations
Physical models never include primary or foreign keys
q.why: Implementation details such as data type names vary with the DBMS.

q.q: At which stage is the physical data model produced?
o: Evaluation
Design
Implementation
Analysis of the data requirements
q.why: The physical model is derived from the logical model during implementation.

q.q: How are many-to-many relationships treated in the two data models?
o: They must be shown in both models as link entities from the start
They are not allowed in either model at any stage
They may appear in the physical model but must be removed from the logical model
They may appear in the logical model but must be resolved before the physical model
q.why: M:N may be shown in the logical model; the physical model needs them resolved into link tables.

q.q: Who is the main audience for a physical data model?
o: Managers, to decide which DBMS to buy
Customers, to show what data is held about them
Developers and the DBA, as instructions to build the database
Users and analysts, to check the data requirements are met
q.why: The physical model tells developers and the DBA how to build it; the logical model is checked by users and analysts.

q.q: What is an entity?
o: A link between two tables, made using a foreign key
One particular record, such as one pupil, in a table
An object, person, place or event about which data is stored
A single data item that describes a person or object
q.why: An entity becomes a table; an attribute is a data item describing it.

q.q: What is an entity occurrence?
o: A relationship that occurs between two entities
The number of times an entity appears on the ER diagram
An attribute that occurs in more than one table
One particular instance of an entity, stored as a record
q.why: An entity occurrence is one instance of the entity, such as one pupil, held as one record.

q.q: Which statement about a foreign key is correct?
o: It must be unique for every record in its own table
It is always part of a composite primary key
It uniquely identifies each record in its own table
It is the primary key of another table and links the two tables
q.why: A foreign key references another table's primary key; many rows may share the same value.

q.q: Why is Surname a poor choice of primary key for a Pupil table?
o: Two pupils can share the same surname
It cannot be indexed for searching
It must be stored as a number
It is too short to be a primary key
q.why: A primary key must be unique for every record, now and in the future.

q.q: A table Result(StudentID, ExamID, Mark) records one mark per student per exam. What is its primary key?
o: Mark alone
StudentID alone
A composite key of StudentID and ExamID
ExamID alone
q.why: A student sits many exams and each exam has many students, so only the pair is unique.

q.q: Why is an email address not an ideal primary key?
o: It can never be unique for each person
It can change, and a primary key should be stable
It cannot be stored as text in a database
It is always too short to identify a person
q.why: A primary key should not need to change; people change email addresses.

q.q: In a cinema booking system, which is most likely to be an attribute rather than an entity?
o: Screening
Seat price
Film
Customer
q.why: A price is a single value describing something else, so it is an attribute.

q.q: What is a secondary key?
o: The foreign key in the many side of a relationship
A non-unique field indexed for fast searching or sorting
A second primary key added to the same table
Any field that could uniquely identify a record
q.why: A secondary key, such as Surname, is indexed for searching but need not be unique.

q.q: What is a candidate key?
o: The attribute chosen from the possible keys to be the primary key of the table
A non-unique field that is indexed to speed up searching and sorting
A primary key copied into another table so the two tables can be linked
Any attribute or minimal set of attributes that could uniquely identify every record
q.why: A candidate key could be the primary key; the primary key is the candidate key chosen.

q.q: Which rule is broken if two records in a Pupil table have the same PupilID?
o: Entity integrity
Referential integrity
Cascade update
Data independence
q.why: Entity integrity requires primary keys to be unique and not null.

q.q: An OrderLine record refers to ProductID P99, but no product P99 exists. What is this?
o: A repeating group breaking 1NF
A composite key breaking entity integrity
A partial dependency breaking 2NF
An orphan record breaking referential integrity
q.why: The foreign key has no matching primary key, so the row is an orphan.

q.q: A customer's address is stored in the Orders table on every order. What is this an example of?
o: A composite key
Data redundancy
Referential integrity
Data independence
q.why: The same address is stored unnecessarily many times.

q.q: Which statement best describes data inconsistency?
o: The same data item is stored in more than one table
Two copies of the same data item hold different values
A required field has been left empty
The data is held in a flat file
q.why: Inconsistency means the duplicated copies no longer match; duplication alone is redundancy.

q.q: What is referential integrity?
o: Every primary key value must be unique and not null
Every attribute must depend on the whole primary key
Every table must be linked to every other table
Every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value
q.why: Referential integrity stops a table contradicting another; unique, non-null keys are entity integrity.

q.q: Deleting an order should automatically delete all its order lines. Which referential integrity option does this?
o: Cascade update
Cascade delete
Set null
Restrict
q.why: Cascade delete removes child records when the parent is deleted.

q.q: A customer with unpaid orders must never be deleted. Which referential integrity option should be set?
o: Restrict (no action)
Cascade delete
Cascade update
Set null
q.why: Restrict refuses to delete a parent that still has children.

q.q: How is the link between data duplication and data inconsistency best explained?
o: Duplication and inconsistency are two names for the same problem
Duplication can lead to inconsistency when one copy is updated and another is not
Inconsistency only occurs when there is no duplication
Inconsistency causes duplication when data is typed in twice
q.why: Redundancy is the duplication; inconsistency is a consequence of it when copies disagree.

q.q: In crow's foot notation, what does the three-pronged end of a line show?
o: An optional relationship
A one-to-one link
The primary key of the entity
The many end of the relationship
q.why: The crow's foot marks the many end; a plain end means one.

q.q: A school bus route has many stops, and each stop is served by many routes. What is the degree of the relationship?
o: Many-to-many
One-to-one
Many-to-one
One-to-many
q.why: Many in both directions gives many-to-many.

q.q: An ER diagram shows Owner with a crow's foot at the Pet end. Which table contains the foreign key?
o: Both tables
Neither table
Owner
Pet
q.why: The foreign key goes at the many end of a one-to-many relationship.

q.q: Why can a many-to-many relationship not be implemented directly in a relational database?
o: A field would have to hold a list of key values
SQL cannot join more than two tables
A table cannot have more than one foreign key
Primary keys must always be numeric
q.why: Fields must be atomic, so a list of links has nowhere to go.

q.q: How is a many-to-many relationship resolved?
o: A foreign key is placed in both entities
The two entities are merged into one table
One of the two entities is deleted from the model
A link entity is added, giving two one-to-many relationships
q.why: A link entity holds one pairing per record, with both crow's feet pointing at it.

q.q: What is usually the primary key of a link entity?
o: The primary key of the first entity alone
A composite of the two foreign keys
A foreign key from one entity plus a date
A new attribute that is not a key in any other table
q.why: The link entity's key is usually the two foreign keys together, e.g. (PupilID, CourseID).

q.q: How do ER modelling and normalisation differ in approach?
o: Both are bottom-up, starting from the attributes
ER modelling is bottom-up; normalisation is top-down
Both are top-down, starting from the entities
ER modelling is top-down; normalisation is bottom-up
q.why: ER modelling starts from real-world things; normalisation starts from the attributes on a document.

q.q: Result(StudentID, ModuleID, StudentName, Mark) has a composite key of StudentID and ModuleID. Which describes StudentName?
o: A candidate key
Fully dependent
Partially dependent
Transitively dependent
q.why: StudentName depends on StudentID only, which is part of the composite key.

q.q: Car(Reg, Model, Manufacturer, ManufacturerCountry) has Reg as its key. Which describes ManufacturerCountry?
o: Transitively dependent on Reg through Manufacturer
Fully dependent on the whole primary key Reg
Partially dependent on part of a composite key
Part of a repeating group of manufacturers
q.why: Reg determines Manufacturer, which determines ManufacturerCountry.

q.q: Which kind of table can never contain a partial dependency?
o: One with a composite primary key
One with a single-attribute primary key
Any table that is in 1NF
A link table
q.why: There is no part of a single-attribute key for anything to depend on.

q.q: What is a repeating group?
o: A field that holds a calculated value
Attributes that occur several times for one value of the key
Two tables that have the same primary key
A field that is copied into another table as a foreign key
q.why: A repeating group is a set of attributes with many values per key, shown in braces in UNF.

q.q: Which describes a table in first normal form?
o: It has a primary key, atomic attributes and no repeating groups
It has no partial dependencies on a composite key
It contains a repeating group shown in braces
It has no non-key attribute depending on another non-key attribute
q.why: 1NF needs a key, atomic values and no repeating groups.

q.q: What does it mean for an attribute to be atomic?
o: It holds one value that cannot be split further
It appears in only one table in the database
It is a key value that can never be changed
It depends on the whole of the primary key
q.why: Atomic values are single, indivisible values.

q.q: What does ProductID followed by an arrow to ProductName mean?
o: ProductID is a foreign key referencing ProductName
Each ProductID is associated with exactly one ProductName
Each ProductName is associated with exactly one ProductID
ProductName is part of a composite key with ProductID
q.why: A functional dependency A to B means each value of A gives exactly one value of B; A is the determinant.

q.q: A table is in 3NF. Which phrase sums up how every non-key attribute depends on the key?
o: On the key, the whole key and nothing but the key
On the key, or on any other non-key attribute
On the foreign keys, the whole key and the index
On part of the key, but never on another attribute
q.why: 3NF means no partial and no transitive dependencies.

q.q: A new tutor cannot be entered into a database until they are assigned a class. Which problem is this?
o: An update anomaly
A deletion anomaly
An insertion anomaly
A referential integrity error
q.why: Being unable to add data because unrelated data is missing is an insertion anomaly.

q.q: What is the main purpose of normalisation?
o: To minimise data redundancy and prevent anomalies
To remove the need for primary keys in tables
To make every table hold as many fields as possible
To make queries need fewer joins between tables
q.why: Normalisation removes unnecessary duplication and the anomalies it causes.

q.q: Which is a valid drawback of a highly normalised design?
o: It leads to more redundant data in the tables
It does not allow primary keys in link tables
Queries may need many joins, which can be slower
It causes more update anomalies when data changes
q.why: More tables means more joins for combined views.

q.q: The price of eggs is stored in two rows. It is changed in one row but not the other. Which anomaly is this?
o: Deletion anomaly
Insertion anomaly
Update anomaly
Partial anomaly
q.why: An update applied to only some copies leaves two prices for one product.

q.q: An order is cancelled and its row deleted, and all record of that customer is lost. Which anomaly is this?
o: Update anomaly
Deletion anomaly
Orphan anomaly
Insertion anomaly
q.why: Deleting one fact unintentionally removes another.

q.q: Why might designers of a data warehouse deliberately denormalise some tables?
o: To save storage space by removing all of the foreign keys
To make update and deletion anomalies impossible
To keep some duplication so read-heavy queries need fewer joins
To remove all primary keys so that data loads faster
q.why: Denormalising is a trade-off: fewer joins for reporting at the cost of some duplication.

q.q: When moving the repeating group to a new table at 1NF, what must go with it?
o: The determinant of any transitive dependency
A calculated total for each group
The original table's primary key
All the other non-key attributes
q.why: The original key links each row back to its parent.

q.q: Why are values such as LineTotal normally left out when normalising?
o: They are not atomic, so they break first normal form
They can be calculated from other attributes
They are always foreign keys to another table
SQL cannot store decimal values such as totals
q.why: Derived data can be calculated when needed, so storing it adds redundancy.

q.q: Which table can contain a partial dependency?
o: Only a table with a single-field key
Any table that contains a foreign key
Only a table that is already in 3NF
Only a table with a composite primary key
q.why: Partial means dependent on part of the key, so the key must have parts.

q.q: When removing a transitive dependency, what must remain in the original table?
o: Nothing, as the tables are now independent
All of the attributes that were moved out
The determinant, such as CustID, as a foreign key
A new composite key made from both tables
q.why: The determinant stays behind to link the tables.

q.q: At 1NF the order form gives OrderLine(OrderNo, ProductID, ProductName, UnitPrice, Qty). Which attribute stays in OrderLine at 2NF?
o: Qty
OrderDate
ProductName
UnitPrice
q.why: Qty needs both parts of the key; ProductName and UnitPrice depend on ProductID alone.

q.q: Order(OrderNo, OrderDate, CustID, CustName, CustTown) is in 2NF. Why is it not in 3NF?
o: CustID should be part of a composite key with OrderNo
OrderDate depends on only part of a composite key
CustName and CustTown depend on CustID, a non-key attribute
It contains a repeating group of products
q.why: OrderNo to CustID to CustName is a transitive chain, so the customer details move out.

q.q: The Fermanagh Fresh order form is normalised to 3NF. Which set of tables results?
o: Order, Product and OrderLine only
Customer, Product and OrderLine only
Customer, Order, Product and OrderLine
Customer, Order and OrderLine only
q.why: The final design has Customer, Order (with CustID*), Product and OrderLine.

q.q: A pupil moves CustName and CustTown into a Customer table at 3NF but removes CustID from Order. What is the problem?
o: Order now has a repeating group
OrderLine now has a partial dependency
The Customer table has no primary key
Orders can no longer be linked to customers
q.why: CustID must stay in Order as a foreign key to keep the link.

q.q: In SESSION-MEMBER(SessionID, MemberID, MemberName, Attended), which attribute shows a partial dependency?
o: Attended
SessionID
MemberName
MemberID
q.why: MemberName depends on MemberID only, which is part of the composite key.

q.q: Why does Attended stay in SESSION-MEMBER at 2NF?
o: It is a derived value that can be calculated
It is part of a repeating group
It depends on both SessionID and MemberID
It is a foreign key to the Member table
q.why: Attendance is a fact about one member at one session.

q.q: At 3NF, CoachName is moved to a COACH table. What must stay in SESSION?
o: CoachName as a foreign key
CoachID as a foreign key
MemberID as a foreign key
Nothing about the coach
q.why: The determinant stays behind to keep the link.

q.q: A coaching register is normalised to 3NF. Which set of tables results?
o: Session, Coach, Member and Session-Member
Session, Member and Attendance only
Coach, Member and Session-Coach
Session, Coach and Member only
q.why: The pattern is event, person in charge, participant and the link entity.

q.q: In order or invoice data, where does Quantity belong in the 3NF design?
o: In the link entity ORDER-PRODUCT
In the CUSTOMER table, beside CustID
In the PRODUCT table, beside UnitPrice
In the ORDER table, beside OrderDate
q.why: Quantity describes the pairing of an order and a product, so it stays in the link entity.

q.q: When the 3NF tables are turned into an ER model, how do the foreign keys appear?
o: As one-to-many relationships with the crow's foot at the table holding the foreign key
As one-to-one relationships, with a plain line at both ends of each link
As many-to-many relationships, with crow's feet at both ends of each link
As attributes drawn inside the parent entity's box on the diagram
q.why: Each foreign key becomes a 1:M relationship with the many end at the table that holds it.

q.q: Which of these is NOT stored in a data dictionary?
o: A validation rule for a field
The data type of a field
The primary key of a table
A customer's actual address
q.why: The data dictionary holds metadata, not the data values themselves.

q.q: How does the DBMS use the data dictionary?
o: To store backup copies of all of the records in each table
To record every change that users make to each record
To check requests against field definitions, rules and permissions
To encrypt the personal data held in each of the tables
q.why: The DBMS refers to the metadata to enforce rules, check permissions and choose indexes.

q.q: What is metadata?
o: Data that has no primary key
Data that is stored on a web server
Data that describes other data
Data that has been deleted from a table
q.why: Metadata is data about data.

q.q: Which data dictionary component records a value filled in automatically when a new record is created?
o: Default value
Lookup
Input mask
Validation rule
q.why: A default value, such as ReorderLevel defaulting to 50, is entered automatically.

q.q: A data dictionary entry says a postcode must be entered as LL00 0LL. Which component is this?
o: Format / input mask
Field size
Lookup
Validation rule
q.why: A format or input mask controls how values look when entered or shown.

q.q: A question asks for three items of metadata. Which answer gains all three marks?
o: Field name, data type and validation rule
Integer, text and Boolean
ProductName, ReorderLevel and Qty
Qty > 0, Price > 0 and Age < 100
q.why: Three distinct items are needed, not three examples of one item.

q.q: Which of these is a DDL command?
o: UPDATE
ALTER TABLE
SELECT
INSERT
q.why: ALTER TABLE changes structure, so it is data definition language.

q.q: Which constraint enforces referential integrity?
o: CHECK
FOREIGN KEY ... REFERENCES
UNIQUE
NOT NULL
q.why: The foreign key constraint makes sure a value exists in the parent table.

q.q: Which data type is most suitable for a price such as 12.50?
o: CHAR(5)
BOOLEAN
INT
DECIMAL(6,2)
q.why: DECIMAL stores exact values with a fixed number of decimal places.

q.q: Why should a phone number be stored as VARCHAR rather than INT?
o: It can start with 0 and is never used in calculations
It is always exactly ten digits long
INT cannot store numbers larger than 999
VARCHAR uses less storage than INT for any number
q.why: Phone numbers are text: a leading 0 would be lost as a number, and they are not used in arithmetic.

q.q: What is the largest value DECIMAL(6,2) can hold?
q.why: Six digits in total, two after the point, gives up to 9999.99.

q.q: Why must the Customer table be created before the CustOrder table that refers to it?
o: The child table must hold more fields than the parent
CustOrder needs Customer's data to be inserted first
The FOREIGN KEY must reference a table that already exists
Tables must be created in alphabetical order
q.why: A foreign key constraint can only reference a parent table that exists.

q.q: What is the effect of DROP TABLE OrderLine; ?
o: It removes the last row added to the table
It removes all the data but keeps the empty table
It removes the primary key from the table
It removes the table and all of its data
q.why: DROP deletes the table and its data; DELETE FROM without WHERE empties the rows but keeps the table.

q.q: Which condition finds postcodes beginning with BT74?
o: Postcode LIKE 'BT74%'
Postcode = 'BT74%'
Postcode LIKE 'BT74_'
Postcode LIKE '%BT74'
q.why: LIKE with % after the fixed part matches anything that starts with BT74; _ matches exactly one character.

q.q: Which values does WHERE Price BETWEEN 2 AND 5 include?
o: Values greater than 2 and less than 5 only
Values from 2 to 5, including 2 and 5
Values below 2 or above 5
Only the values 2 and 5
q.why: BETWEEN is inclusive at both ends.

q.q: A query joins Customer (4 rows) and CustOrder (4 rows) but the join condition is left out. How many rows are returned?
q.why: Every row is paired with every row, a Cartesian product of 4 x 4.

q.q: What does the wildcard _ match in a LIKE pattern?
o: One or more characters
Any number of characters, including none
Exactly one character
Any single digit only
q.why: In standard SQL, _ is exactly one character and % is any number of characters.

q.q: Which query lists the title and author of every science book?
o: SELECT Title, Author WHERE Category = 'Science' FROM Book;
SELECT Book FROM Title, Author WHERE Category = 'Science';
SELECT Title, Author FROM Book WHERE Category = 'Science';
SELECT Title, Author FROM Book WHERE Category = Science;
q.why: Fields after SELECT, table after FROM, then WHERE, with text in quotes.

q.q: How is WHERE YearGroup = 13 AND House = 'Erne' OR House = 'Fermanagh' evaluated with no brackets?
o: YearGroup = 13 AND (House = 'Erne' OR House = 'Fermanagh')
It produces an error because brackets are required
(YearGroup = 13 AND House = 'Erne') OR House = 'Fermanagh'
(YearGroup = 13 OR House = 'Erne') AND House = 'Fermanagh'
q.why: AND is evaluated before OR, so Fermanagh pupils from every year would be included.

q.q: In ORDER BY Merits DESC, Surname ASC, when does Surname affect the order?
o: Only for pupils with no Merits recorded
For every pupil, before Merits is sorted
Never, as only the first sort key is used
Only for pupils with equal Merits
q.why: The second sort key only decides the order of rows that tie on the first.

q.q: A pupil writes WHERE Surname = 'Mc%' to find surnames starting with Mc. What will happen?
o: It finds all surnames that start with Mc
It looks for someone literally called Mc%
It finds all surnames that end with Mc
It produces a syntax error
q.why: Wildcards only work with LIKE; with = the % is treated as an ordinary character.

q.q: Which query counts the pupils in each house?
o: SELECT House, COUNT(*) FROM Pupil GROUP BY House;
SELECT COUNT(House) FROM Pupil WHERE House;
SELECT House, COUNT(*) FROM Pupil ORDER BY House;
SELECT House, SUM(*) FROM Pupil GROUP BY House;
q.why: GROUP BY makes one group per house and COUNT(*) counts the rows in each.

q.q: What is the effect of DELETE FROM Booking; ?
o: It deletes every record in Booking but keeps the table
It produces an error because WHERE is missing
It deletes the first record in Booking only
It deletes the Booking table and its structure
q.why: Without WHERE every row matches; the empty table remains.

q.q: Which statement changes the town of customer C101 to Omagh?
o: UPDATE Customer SET CustTown = 'Omagh' WHERE CustID = 'C101';
ALTER TABLE Customer SET CustTown = 'Omagh' WHERE CustID = 'C101';
UPDATE Customer WHERE CustID = 'C101' SET CustTown = 'Omagh';
INSERT INTO Customer (CustTown) VALUES ('Omagh') WHERE CustID = 'C101';
q.why: UPDATE ... SET ... WHERE changes existing values, with SET before WHERE.

q.q: Why might the DBMS reject INSERT INTO CustOrder VALUES (5009, '2026-10-20', 'C999'); ?
o: INSERT statements always need a WHERE clause
C999 does not exist in Customer, breaking referential integrity
Dates cannot be inserted using an INSERT statement
OrderNo must be stored as text in quotation marks
q.why: The foreign key has no matching parent record.

q.q: INSERT INTO Contact (ContactName, Email) VALUES ('Green', 'green@example.co.uk'); is run on a table that also has a Phone field with no constraints. What happens to Phone?
o: It is set to zero
The insert is rejected
It is left empty (null)
It copies the Email value
q.why: Fields not given a value are left null, unless a NOT NULL constraint stops the insert.

q.q: Which statement raises all Fruit prices by 10%?
o: UPDATE Product SET UnitPrice = UnitPrice + 10 WHERE Category = 'Fruit';
UPDATE Product SET UnitPrice = UnitPrice * 1.10;
UPDATE Product SET UnitPrice = UnitPrice * 1.10 WHERE Category = 'Fruit';
UPDATE Product SET UnitPrice = UnitPrice * 0.10 WHERE Category = 'Fruit';
q.why: Multiplying by 1.10 adds 10%; leaving out WHERE would change every product.

q.q: How should a single field in a record be blanked?
o: INSERT NULL INTO field
DELETE field FROM table
DROP field FROM table
UPDATE ... SET field = NULL
q.why: DELETE removes whole rows; to blank one field, use UPDATE with SET field = NULL.

q.q: Which is safe practice before running a DELETE with a WHERE clause?
o: Drop the table first and then recreate it afterwards from a backup
Run the DELETE without a WHERE clause first to test that it works
Remove the primary key so the matching rows can be found more easily
Run a SELECT with the same WHERE to see which rows will be affected
q.why: Checking the rows with SELECT first, and using a transaction, avoids deleting the wrong data.

q.q: What does QBE generate automatically from the user's grid?
o: An ER diagram
The equivalent SQL
A data dictionary
A new table
q.why: The DBMS builds the SQL behind the scenes, which can be viewed.

q.q: Which is an advantage of SQL over QBE?
o: It lets users drag fields into a grid to build queries
It is always quicker for an untrained user to build a query
It has no syntax to learn, so beginners can use it at once
It is an industry standard, so queries are portable between DBMSs
q.why: Each product's QBE screen is different; SQL works the same across DBMSs.

q.q: A receptionist with no database training needs to find all bookings for one date. Which is most suitable?
o: The data dictionary
QBE
SQL typed at a command line
A CREATE TABLE statement
q.why: QBE needs little technical knowledge and no syntax.

q.q: Why does QBE avoid syntax errors?
o: It checks each query against the ER diagram
The SQL is generated automatically and correctly
It uses a standard grid that works in every DBMS
It only allows SELECT * queries
q.why: QBE builds the SQL for the user, so there is no mistyping.

q.q: A developer needs a web application to run queries on a database. Which is most suitable and why?
o: QBE, because it is used interactively with a visual grid
SQL, because it needs no syntax to be learned
QBE, because it is the industry standard across DBMSs
SQL, because it can be embedded in programs and web applications
q.why: QBE is interactive only; SQL can be embedded in programs.

q.q: Which task can SQL do directly that QBE usually cannot?
o: Filter records by criteria
Sort the results
Choose fields to show
Create and alter tables
q.why: CREATE TABLE and ALTER TABLE build the database; QBE usually uses a separate design view.
